gaps.fact: Historically Murcia's Monastrell vines were ungrafted because of the sandy soil. Only the article and the country overview teach it; no chapter fact or stem.

Txakoli is made in modern temperature controlled stainless steel tanks; and the DO Pago estates make mainly international styles of red. The first is taught nowhere; the second only in the la-mancha article.

The three Txakoli DOs by name: Bizkaiko Txakolina, Arabako Txakolina and Getariako Txakolina. Only Getariako is ever named; c-5znp51hu describes the other two by their ground, and the Village Spain chapter never mentions Txakoli at all.
Juan Gil, the Court's Murcia house, stands only in the jumilla-yecla article; no stem and no producer entry.
Murcia avoided phylloxera until the 1980s (it reached Jumilla in 1989). Only the article gives it; no chapter fact or stem.
How many Vinos de Pago there are (the Court prints 20 as of 2022). No count appears anywhere in the Codex; a dated card is the right home, since the number keeps rising (see the court update).
Txakoli whites are traditionally served with oily seafood. The one stem calls Txakoli an aperitif; no line pairs it with anchovies, sardines or other oily fish.

errors.where: js/regions/spain.json, records.spain.traps[5]: "Vino de Pago is a single estate's own appellation, not a tier above DOCa in prestige by law; it sits beside the DOs." With the same record's exam[0] and the REGIONS.countries.spain card "Spain's quality pyramid, top down": DOCa/DOQ, Vino de Pago, DO, Vino de Calidad, Vino de la Tierra, Vino.
errors.claim: Vino de Pago sits beside the DOs, below DOCa in the pyramid.
errors.correction: The 2003 wine law lists the levels of the origin system in ascending order and puts vinos de pagos last, after DOCa, and a pago inside a qualified region takes the name Vino de Pago Calificado (as c-uolx1t26 teaches). The Codex itself places it at the top elsewhere: the Village Spain chapter lists it first (fact 1), the Classifications & Labels chapter puts it at the top beside DOCa (fact 4), INTRO_CLASS says it sits at the very top, and the la-mancha trap calls it above DO in prestige. The Court asks for the place of DO Pago in the hierarchy, so one teaching should stand everywhere: the single estate DOP at the head of the ladder, a level of its own for one property rather than a rung a region climbs to.
errors.source: Ley 24/2003, de 10 de julio, de la Viña y del Vino, article 13 (the levels of the origin system); the Codex's own Village Spain chapter fact 1, Classifications & Labels fact 4, INTRO_CLASS Spain and js/regions/spain.json records.la-mancha.traps.

courtUpdates.printed: DO Pago: Vinos de Pagos was first created in 2003. There are 20 Vinos de Pagos as of 2022, serving the purpose of producer appellations outside of traditional winemaking styles.
courtUpdates.now: About 26 Vinos de Pago by May 2025 (13 in Castilla-La Mancha, 4 in Navarra, 4 in Valencia, 3 in Castilla y León, 2 in Aragón, by the count FENAVIN published), with Tharsys in Valencia registered by the European Union on 2 October 2025, which an unofficial count puts at 28. Castilla-La Mancha still holds half of them, so the Court's location cell stands.
courtUpdates.source: FENAVIN press note on the Vinos de Pago, May 2025 (fenavin.com); winewitandwisdomswe.com, 8 October 2025 (Tharsys, unofficial count); the European register eAmbrosia is the authority to confirm the total.
